newsitem.title: BELGIUM: "Santer" package seen slashing EU grain prices.
newsitem.headline: "Santer" package seen slashing EU grain prices.

text.p: A further sharp cut in grain intervention prices with a corresponding increase in direct compensation payments to farmers is envisaged in a package of measures to prepare for EU expansion eastwards, EU sources said on Thursday.
"Price cuts and compensation are the key (grain) issues," said a Commission source.
Another source said that a 20 percent cut in intervention prices from the current level of 119.19 ecus a tonne balanced by a 24 ecus a tonne to 78 ecus a tonne increase in compensation was envisaged.
Under the 1992 EU farm reform, grain intervention prices were cut by 30 percent over three years.
But the source cautioned that these were just draft figures which were likely to change before EU Commission President Jacques Santer presents the package in Strasbourg on July 16.
The price cuts, if accepted, would help bring EU prices down to world market levels and enable the EU to export without subsidies.
Otherwise, Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler has warned that cereal set-aside may have to rise to 25 percent, from five percent, in order to prevent huge surpluses reappearing.
Such an increase is seen as politically unacceptable.

Agricultural reforms, mainly in the cereals and beef sectors, will be one element of the four-part package. The other elements are: - Budget spending guidelines from 1999 to 2005 in agriculture and other sectors. - Reform of EU structural funds for regional, social and agricultural development. - Impact of entry of up to 10 former communist east European countries on EU agricultural and other policies.

On Wednesday, Fischler's chief aid, Corrado Pirzio-Biroli, warned that without reform EU cereal intervention stocks would surge to 58 million tonnes by 2005 -- over 65 percent above the previous highest level.
Beef stocks are also seen climbing to 1.5 million tonnes by 2005, from around 430,000 tonnes at the end of 1996, he told the Centre for European Policy Studies.
The EU would be unable to offload surplus stocks onto world markets because of World Trade Organisation (WTO) curbs on subsidised exports, Pirzio-Biroli warned.
